title: Starting a Hospice Agency in Washington: Licensing, Costs, and Step-by-Step Guide

html:
Introduction

Starting a Hospice Agency in Washington represents a meaningful opportunity to serve individuals and families requiring compassionate end-of-life care while building a compliant, sustainable care business. This vital service provides comprehensive symptom management, palliative care, and crucial emotional and spiritual support. Oversight and funding are administered by the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), with reimbursement and program funding coordinated through the Washington State Health Care Authority (HCA) for Medicaid recipients.

With an established market of over 400 licensed in-home service agencies and significant opportunities in high-demand niches like pediatric and rural telehealth hospice, Washington offers a competitive but rewarding landscape for providers. Reimbursement rates, such as the Medicaid routine home care rate of approximately $225 per day and up to $1,619 per day for continuous care, create a viable financial model. This market is ideal for providers prepared to navigate the state’s rigorous Certificate of Need (CON) process, licensing, staffing, and ongoing compliance requirements.

This guide walks you through every step of launching a Hospice Agency in Washington, from understanding complex regulations and the CON process to staffing your interdisciplinary team, managing reimbursement, and preparing for state and federal inspections. Whether you are an experienced healthcare professional or an entrepreneur with a passion for compassionate care, this framework will provide the clarity needed to succeed.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Washington’s Hospice Agency Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Your Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility or Office
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Referral Development
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews
  • Frequently Asked Questions

Section 1: Understand Washington’s Hospice Agency Regulations

Washington regulates Hospice Agencies through the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), specifically its Health Systems Quality Assurance (HSQA) Division. The DOH is responsible for overseeing compliance with state laws (WAC 246-335), issuing licenses, and conducting surveys to ensure patient safety and quality of care. A critical and often challenging prerequisite in Washington is obtaining a Certificate of Need (CON), which demonstrates that a new hospice service is necessary to meet the needs of the community. This process precedes the actual license application.

Providers serving Medicaid or Medicare populations must also comply with federal frameworks, most notably the Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoPs) for Hospice Care. These federal rules are extensive and set the national standard for hospice operations, including the structure of the interdisciplinary group, patient rights, and quality reporting. Compliance with HIPAA for patient privacy is also mandatory.

The regulatory framework in Washington emphasizes comprehensive end-of-life care quality, patient and family rights, effective interdisciplinary team management, and robust pain and symptom control. Licenses are granted after the CON is approved and a successful initial survey is completed. Licenses typically require renewal every one year, contingent on a successful renewal application and continued compliance.

Section 2: Choose the Type and Size of Your Program

Washington supports multiple levels of hospice care, which are defined by federal regulations and are essential to your service model. Each has different staffing, documentation, and reimbursement requirements. You must be prepared to offer all four levels of care, even if some are provided through contractual arrangements.

  • Routine Home Care (RHC): This is the most common level of hospice care, provided in the patient’s place of residence (private home, assisted living facility, or nursing home). It includes nursing, aide services, social work, and spiritual support.
  • Continuous Home Care (CHC): Provided during periods of medical crisis to manage acute symptoms. This level requires a minimum of eight hours of direct nursing care in a 24-hour period, primarily delivered by an RN or LPN.
  • General Inpatient Care (GIP): Short-term care provided in a contracted hospital, skilled nursing facility, or dedicated hospice inpatient unit for pain or symptoms that cannot be managed in the home setting.
  • Inpatient Respite Care: Short-term inpatient care (up to five consecutive days) provided to give the patient’s primary caregiver a rest.

Beyond these required levels, strategic providers can find success by focusing on high-demand niches. The report highlights opportunities in pediatric hospice, telehealth-supported rural outreach, and culturally tailored care programs designed for specific communities. Program size is measured by Average Daily Census (ADC), with new agencies often starting with caseloads ranging from 10 to over 100 patients, depending on staffing capacity and service area. Demand is strongest in populous urban centers like the Seattle-Tacoma-Bellevue metropolitan area, while rural counties in Eastern Washington may offer entry opportunities with less competition, especially for providers leveraging telehealth.

Section 3: Business Structure and Licensing

Before you can provide care, you must establish a formal business entity and navigate Washington’s multi-stage licensing process. Providers typically operate as a Limited Liability Company (LLC) or S-Corporation to protect personal assets. The foundational steps include:

  • Register your business with the Washington Secretary of State.
  • Obtain an Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS.
  • Secure required insurance, including general liability, professional liability (malpractice), and workers’ compensation.
  • Apply for a Certificate of Need (CON) from the DOH. This is a competitive and data-intensive process where you must prove a community need for your agency. It involves detailed financial projections, service area analysis, and demonstrating your capability to operate.
  • Submit a licensing application to the DOH HSQA Division after your CON has been approved. This application includes your policies and procedures, staffing plan, and proof of financial viability.

Licensing timelines in Washington are significantly longer than in many other states due to the CON requirement. The entire process, from starting the CON application to receiving your license, generally ranges from 12 to 24 months, and can be longer depending on CON review cycles, potential legal challenges from competitors, and the completeness of your application.

Section 4: Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A robust business plan is essential for securing funding and navigating the CON process. Startup costs for a hospice agency in Washington typically range from $100,000 to $250,000. This includes costs for CON consultation and legal fees, business formation, office rent, initial payroll, electronic medical record (EMR) software, and insurance premiums.

Operating expenses are driven primarily by your interdisciplinary team. Staffing represents 60-70% of total operating costs, making recruitment and retention a critical business function. Your revenue will come from per diem reimbursement rates paid by Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurers.

Typical reimbursement or revenue ranges in Washington include:

  • Washington Medicaid Routine Home Care: Approximately $225 per day
  • Washington Medicaid Continuous Home Care: Up to $1,619 per day (billed hourly)
  • Medicare Rates: Federally set and geographically adjusted, with similar tiers for Routine, Continuous, Inpatient, and Respite care.
  • Private Insurance: Rates are negotiated individually with each payer.

Profitability depends on managing your patient census and controlling costs. Providers operating at a target Average Daily Census (ADC) of 25-30 patients can generally achieve 10-25% gross profit margins. Most agencies plan for a break-even point between 12 and 24 months after licensure, depending on how quickly they can build their referral base and patient census.

Section 5: Secure a Suitable Facility or Office

Unlike a residential facility, a hospice agency’s physical location is an administrative office that supports your field staff. However, this office must meet specific requirements to ensure compliance and operational efficiency.

Facility requirements for a hospice agency office include:

  • A secure, professional office space compliant with local business zoning and accessibility codes.
  • HIPAA-compliant storage for patient records, including locked file cabinets for paper charts and secure servers or cloud storage for your EMR system.
  • A dedicated, lockable area for storing medical supplies, personal protective equipment (PPE), and any durable medical equipment.
  • A private conference room for interdisciplinary team meetings, family consultations, and staff training.
  • Reliable high-speed internet and a robust telecommunications system to support field staff and telehealth services.

Your location selection should consider accessibility for your staff, proximity to major hospitals and referral sources, and the availability of a qualified clinical workforce in the surrounding area.

Section 6: Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The heart of any hospice agency is its Interdisciplinary Group (IDG), which is mandated by Medicare and Washington state regulations. This team works together to create and manage a holistic plan of care for each patient.

Required roles for your IDG and administrative team typically include:

  • Administrator/Director: Oversees all agency operations, finances, and compliance.
  • Medical Director: A licensed physician who provides clinical oversight and leads the IDG.
  • Director of Nursing (DON) / Clinical Supervisor: A Registered Nurse (RN) who manages all clinical staff and patient care services.
  • Registered Nurses (RNs): Serve as case managers, providing skilled nursing, assessments, and coordinating the plan of care.
  • Medical Social Workers (MSWs): Address the psychosocial needs of patients and families.
  • Spiritual Counselors/Chaplains: Provide non-denominational spiritual support.
  • Hospice Aides (HHAs/CNAs): Assist patients with personal care and activities of daily living under the supervision of an RN.
  • Bereavement Coordinator: Manages the required bereavement support program for families for up to 13 months after the patient’s death.
  • Volunteer Coordinator: Recruits, trains, and manages a team of volunteers, whose service hours are required by Medicare.

Training is a major focus of regulatory oversight. Hospice aides must complete 75 hours of initial training and pass a competency evaluation. All staff must receive comprehensive orientation on the hospice philosophy, pain and symptom management, infection control, patient rights, and your agency’s specific policies. Ongoing continuing education is also mandated to keep staff current on best practices.

Section 7: Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Your agency cannot operate without a comprehensive set of written policies and procedures that serve as your operational playbook. The DOH will review these documents meticulously during your initial licensing survey. Washington requires written policies covering all aspects of your operation, aligned with WAC 246-335 and the Medicare CoPs.

Key policy areas include:

  • Governing Body and Administration: Defines your organizational structure, mission, and lines of authority.
  • Patient Rights and Responsibilities: Outlines the rights of every patient and family you serve.
  • Admission, Transfer, and Discharge Criteria: Details the specific criteria for accepting patients onto your service and the procedures for discharge.
  • Interdisciplinary Group (IDG) Plan of Care: Governs how the IDG develops, reviews, and updates each patient’s individualized plan of care every 15 days.
  • Pain and Symptom Management: Protocols for assessing and managing patient symptoms effectively.
  • Infection Control and Prevention: A detailed plan to prevent the spread of infectious diseases.
  • Emergency Preparedness Plan: Procedures for continuing operations and protecting patients during natural disasters or other emergencies.
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI): Your framework for continuously monitoring data, identifying problems, and improving care quality.
  • Staffing, Training, and Competency: Policies covering hiring qualifications, orientation, ongoing training, and competency evaluations.
  • Volunteer Program Management: Guidelines for recruiting, training, and utilizing volunteers.
  • Bereavement Services: The plan for providing bereavement support to families.

Individual care plans are the cornerstone of hospice. They must be developed by the IDG in collaboration with the patient and family, reviewed regularly, and meticulously documented to reflect the patient’s changing needs and goals.

Section 8: Marketing and Referral Development

Unlike consumer-facing businesses, hospice marketing is a B2B (business-to-business) effort focused on building trust with professional referral sources. Your reputation for compliance, responsiveness, and high-quality clinical care is your best marketing tool.

Referrals for hospice agencies in Washington typically come from:

  • Hospital discharge planners and case managers
  • Physicians in oncology, cardiology, pulmonology, and primary care
  • Administrators and Directors of Nursing at Skilled Nursing Facilities (SNFs)
  • Executive Directors at Assisted Living and Residential Care Facilities
  • Case managers at Home Health Agencies
  • Geriatric care managers

Successful providers build strong, lasting relationships with these key partners. This involves meeting with them regularly, providing clear and timely communication about mutual patients, and demonstrating excellent clinical outcomes. Focus on being a reliable, responsive partner who makes the referral process seamless and provides peace of mind that their patients will receive exceptional care.

Section 9: Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Reviews

Oversight does not end once you receive your license. Your agency will be subject to periodic inspections from surveying bodies, including the Washington State DOH (HSQA) and potentially a CMS-approved accrediting organization like the Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP) or Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC) if you choose to become accredited.

Surveys can be routine (annual/biennial) or unannounced (often triggered by a complaint). Inspections are focused on identifying deficiencies where your agency fails to meet state or federal regulations. Common deficiencies cited in hospice surveys nationally include:

  • Incomplete, inconsistent, or outdated patient care plans.
  • Failure to conduct or document comprehensive patient assessments in a timely manner.
  • Inadequate coordination of care and documentation of IDG meetings.
  • Medication management and reconciliation errors.
  • Insufficient supervision of hospice aides by a registered nurse.
  • Lack of proper documentation to support the services billed.

A culture of continuous quality improvement and maintaining audit-ready documentation at all times are essential for long-term success and avoiding costly penalties or plans of correction.

Section 10: Frequently Asked Questions

Q: How long does it take to open a Hospice Agency in Washington?

  • A: The licensing process, including the mandatory Certificate of Need (CON) application, is lengthy. You should plan for a timeline of 12 to 24 months or longer, depending on CON approval cycles, the competitiveness of your service area, and the completeness of your application.

Q: What licenses are required to start a hospice agency in Washington?

  • A: You need two primary approvals from the state. First, you must obtain a Certificate of Need (CON). After the CON is granted, you can apply for a Hospice Agency license from the Washington State Department of Health (DOH), which is governed by WAC 246-335.

Q: What reimbursement is available for hospice services in Washington?

  • A: Reimbursement primarily comes from Medicare and Medicaid, which pay a per diem (daily) rate. Washington Medicaid offers rates around $225/day for routine home care and up to $1,619/day for continuous care. Medicare rates are similar and are tiered by the four levels of care. You can also contract with private insurance companies or accept private pay.

Conclusion

Starting a Hospice Agency in Washington is a complex but profoundly rewarding endeavor. It requires careful planning to navigate the Certificate of Need process, a deep understanding of state and federal regulations, and unwavering operational discipline. The path is challenging, but providers who invest in compliance, build a strong interdisciplinary team, and cultivate trusted referral relationships are positioned to create a lasting, positive impact on their communities and build a successful business.
